checks.text: A 70B+ model on one GPU is not a training plan. Use a smaller model, or use the large model only as a teacher or a baseline.
Pretraining from scratch needs a cluster and weeks. For your budget, start from an open base model and continue from there.
Repository-level tasks are demanding for small models. Check that your baseline solves a non-trivial share of tasks before you spend on RL, and consider function-level goals first.

Many execution-verified RL task sets in this catalog are Python-centric. Check the languages field of each pick, and expect to lean on SFT and multi-language evals such as MultiPL-E for other languages.
Instruction tuning can change how a model handles fill-in-the-middle prompts. Evaluate completion directly (SAFIM, CrossCodeEval) before and after.
Private code: scan for secrets and personal data, check licenses and your own policy, and never put it in a shared dataset or an eval you publish.

steps.title: Measure first
body: Score the model you have, before you change anything. Freeze prompt, temperature, number of samples and harness version, and report pass@1 from several samples.
Add one private eval of 50 to 200 tasks from your own domain, with tests, that never enters training.

picks.why: Dated problems: score only those published after the model's training cutoff.
Quick smoke test for function writing. Classic and likely contaminated, so never your only number.
Harder function-level tasks that call real libraries.
HumanEval and MBPP translated into many languages.
Instructional code editing.
Syntax-aware fill-in-the-middle.
Cross-file completion.
Refreshing real-issue tasks, a better gate against memorization than the original.
Still the common reference point, but OpenAI stopped reporting it after finding many flawed tests (see its page). Use it to compare with published numbers, not as your only gate.
Terminal tasks with tests.
Edit-and-run tasks across several languages.
Enterprise-style SQL workflows.
Text-to-SQL with execution match.
Formal Olympiad-style statements in Lean.
Harder formal problems from the Putnam competition.

pitfalls.t: Compare like with like. Different harnesses and prompts give different scores for the same model.

steps.title: Fix data quality before adding more data
body: Deduplicate, decontaminate against your evals, and filter by license. Do this to every dataset you plan to mix, not only your own.

body.t: Private corpus: also redact secrets and personal data.

picks.why: MinHash dedup and filtering pipelines that run locally or on a cluster.
Decontamination against eval sets.
License detection for source files.
PII detection and redaction (a general tool, check it fits source code).

pitfalls.t: Plain n-gram decontamination misses rephrased copies. Keep a private eval and a time-windowed one.

steps.title: Choose the starting model
body: Start from the strongest open model you can afford to train, whose license fits your use. A strong base carries most of the signal, so your job is to add to it, not to rebuild it.

body.t: You chose a base model: continue with SFT. A base model needs a chat template and instruction data first.

picks.why: Small, Apache-2.0, with an open recipe.
Code-specialized family. License verified for the 7B and 32B sizes only.
8B code model, MIT.
Open data and recipe. Check its license terms.
Apache-2.0 base.
14B reasoning model already RL-tuned on code, MIT.
MoE with 3B active parameters. Only trainable at this size with an MoE-capable framework.
Agent-oriented, Apache-2.0.
Fully open, Apache-2.0.
80B MoE (3B active), Apache-2.0.
Open-weight reasoning model with tool use, Apache-2.0.

pitfalls.t: Check the license on the model page, not only here. Some open-weight licenses have revenue or production conditions.

steps.title: Pretrain or continue pretraining
body: This is the expensive stage. Quality filtering has repeatedly beaten raw volume. Deduplicate at file and repository level, and keep license metadata.
Most of these corpora are metadata or gated: expect to fetch contents from Software Heritage or GitHub and to accept terms.

picks.why: Largest open, ungated option in this catalog.
Educational-quality subset, a strong quality-filter reference.
Most transparent end-to-end recipe.
High-quality data for the final annealing phase.

steps.title: Optional: continue pretraining on your own code
body: If you have a large private corpus in a language or framework the base model knows less well, a short continued-pretraining run on a mix of your code and general code can help. Mix in general code to limit forgetting, and re-run your evals, including a general one.

picks.why: Use as the general-code share of the mix.

steps.title: Teach the format with SFT
body: Start small: tens of thousands of checked examples have competed with much larger sets in published work. Train on the response tokens only, use one chat template, and run your evals after.

body.t: One GPU: use LoRA and a small slice of the data. Learning rates and ranks are yours to tune; there is no universal setting.

picks.why: Seeded from real code snippets. Written by an OpenAI model, so check terms.
5M examples with quality scores: take the best slice.
Human commits as instructions, no LLM teacher.
Self-generated and execution-filtered.
Distilled reasoning traces for competitive problems (teacher: DeepSeek-R1).
Large reasoning set with math, code and science.
Codeforces problems with reasoning traces.
Agent trajectories on synthetic SWE tasks. Small sets can matter.
OpenHands trajectories on real tasks.
Terminal agent traces.
Synthetic text-to-SQL.
Large synthetic text-to-SQL corpus.
Formalized problems in Lean.
Lean statements with proofs.

pitfalls.t: Many synthetic sets inherit a teacher's terms and some are non-commercial. Check each pick's license before you train a model you will ship.

steps.title: Optional: preference optimization
body: Only if SFT has plateaued. Pairs where one answer passes tests and the other fails are far more reliable than model-judged pairs. If you can run tests, building on-policy pairs from your own model is often better than any public set. Control for length.

picks.why: Questions with test cases, usable to build pairs and rewards.
Pairs from competitive problems, with pass rates.
Judged by a model: useful for style, weaker on correctness.

steps.title: On one GPU: rejection sampling instead of full RL
body: Full RL needs many rollouts and a trainer you can keep fed. A cheap alternative: sample several solutions per task from your model, run the tests, keep the passing ones, and SFT on them. Repeat once or twice, and re-measure each round.
If you want to try GRPO on one GPU with a small model, the TRL example below shows a unit-test reward on a small dataset.

picks.why: Tasks with tests for filtering samples.
Competitive problems with tests.

pitfalls.t: A subprocess with a timeout is not a security boundary. Run generated code in a container.

steps.title: Reward what passes: RL with verifiable rewards
body: Sample several solutions per task, run the tests, reward passes. The open frameworks below support this. Start from a model that already solves a fair share of tasks, and filter tasks to a middle band of pass rate: tasks the model always or never solves give no signal.
Use the same eval as in step 1 to decide whether it worked, and add a general-coding regression check.

body.t: Repository tasks need a container image per task and a verifier that applies the tests after the agent finishes.

picks.why: Competitive problems with tests.
Ships per-model difficulty fields for filtering. Check the license, which the API does not list.
Competitive problems with improved test cases.
Function problems with test cases.
Pytest-verified tasks with pass-rate fields. Non-commercial license.
Real tasks with environments.
Large synthetic task set.
Executable environments with synthetic tests.
Large, refreshing set of real tasks.
Task format and runner for terminal and agent tasks.
Multi-language repository RL tasks.
SQL with execution match.
Lean statements for prover RL (checked by the Lean compiler).
Widely used RL framework with code-reward support.
Built for multi-turn agent RL.
Large-scale async RL.
Library for defining environments and rewards.

pitfalls.t: Reward hacking is documented: reading git history for the fix, editing tests, fetching solutions from the web. Strip history, hide the tests, and block the network.
Check every task with a reference solution. It must pass, and the unfixed code must fail.

steps.title: Run generated code in a sandbox
body: Every reward and every eval runs code a model wrote. Run it in a container or VM with no network, a read-only filesystem and limits on memory, CPU and processes. On a shared cluster, use rootless containers and ask your admins.

picks.why: The default for a single machine or node.
For HPC clusters where Docker is not allowed.
A ready-made code-execution service for RL rewards.
Stronger isolation for containers.

steps.title: Measure again, and keep what helped
body: Run the same evals with the same settings. Look at the target score, a general-coding regression check, and a few outputs by eye. If something got worse, undo the last change before adding another.
Write down what each stage changed. Your private eval is the tiebreaker.
